title: Preparing SKA Software on French Supercomputers: The DDF Pipeline | Mathis Certenais
description: How the DDF Pipeline is being hardened into production-ready FR SRCNet software, from a computer-science view: what a run consumes, what it produces, and how it scales.
aiSummary: The article locates the DDF Pipeline inside the collaboration hardening it: ECLAT, the joint laboratory for HPC and AI applied to astronomical instrumentation, and ASTRA, the ANR–NumPEx project preparing the French SKA Regional Centre. Read as data logistics, the workflow moves a pointing through five steps, from LOFAR archive sites to a catalogue of four million sources; read as a resource budget, one run consumes 38.72 GB compressed and produces 594 GB in 68.8 hours. The parallel version cuts that to 8.7 hours on 24 Jean Zay nodes at 31 % CPU.

citations.title: A description of the radio astronomy data processing tool DDF Pipeline
Enabling Radio Astronomy to Use French Supercomputers

image.alt: The DDF Pipeline, read as a computer scientist

body.text: [ECLAT](https://eclat-lab.fr/en/), the Extreme Computing Lab for Astronomical Telescopes, is a joint laboratory and a centre of excellence for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence applied to astronomical instrumentation. It brings together sixteen laboratories and teams, including CNRS, Inria, Eviden, the OCA and the Observatoire de Paris.

[ASTRA](https://numpex-astra-e5d484.padcpages.obspm.fr/), the ANR–NumPEx project “Alliance for Scalable Techniques in Radio Astronomy”, sits one layer above the software. Led by Marc-Antoine Miville-Deschênes at LPENS, it prepares the technological foundation of the French SKA Regional Centre. The DDF Pipeline is one scientific application inside one ASTRA use case — the Widefield Radio Continuum Surveys case.
The workflow, read as data logistics
The five steps that turn a LOFAR pointing into a science-ready catalogue are, read as a computer scientist, a chain of data volumes moving between sites:

items: **Direction-independent calibration and flagging** runs on the LOFAR Long-Term Archive sites — Amsterdam, Jülich and Poznań — where the raw data live. Dysco compression shrinks an 8-hour pointing to roughly 50 GB.

**Direction-dependent (DDE) calibration and imaging** runs the [DDF Pipeline](https://github.com/mhardcastle/ddf-pipeline) — [killMS](https://github.com/saopicc/killMS) for calibration, [DDFacet](https://github.com/saopicc/DDFacet) for imaging — mostly at the University of Hertfordshire, with smaller volumes at Bologna, Leiden and Hamburg.
**Archived products** total about 120 GB per 8-hour dataset, held on SURF storage in the Netherlands.

**Polarisation and RM-synthesis** run [pyrmsynth](https://github.com/mrbell/pyrmsynth) over about 35 GB of Stokes Q and U FITS per 16 deg² field. The polarisation signal is Fourier-transformed along the frequency axis to recover, for each line of sight, the Faraday rotation measure — the magnetic field between the source and the telescope.

body.text: The widefield case is where the volumes stop being a sequence and become a rate. The ASTRA project states 250 PB of raw data accumulated from 25,000 hours of observations across 3,168 pointing centres, each observed for 8 to 12 hours, feeding 250 publications over five years — and, for the SKA era it is preparing for, an expected data rate of about 2 TB per observation hour. The DDF Pipeline has processed LoTSS routinely since 2016.
What one run consumes and produces

The profiling in [arXiv 2509.03075](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03075) reads the pipeline as a resource budget. One representative run starts from 24 MeasurementSet tar-archives: 38.72 GB compressed, 134.4 GB once decompressed. It produces 594 GB in total, of which the 15 images amount to about 17.92 GB — 11 full-resolution at 1.575 GB each and 4 low-resolution at 0.148 GB each.

The loop is two-stage: 120 killMS calls and 19 DDFacet calls, at a default output of 20,000×20,000 pixels at 1.5 arcsec. On the profiling machine — an HPE ProLiant DL385 Gen10 Plus with two AMD EPYC 7543 32-core processors and 512 GB of RAM, half of it configured as shared memory — a single node takes 68.87 hours. That time splits 53.40 % to killMS, 33.87 % to DDFacet, and the remaining 12.09 % across steps the profiler did not label — most likely DDFacet or killMS sub-stages rather than idle time.

The parallel version ran on the Jean Zay cpu partition — 24 nodes, 960 CPUs — over an 8-hour integration LOFAR dataset, as reported in [the SC26 paper](https://doi.ieeecomputersociety.org/10.1109/SCW72768.2026.00093). It finished in 8.7 hours, about 7.9× faster than the 68.8-hour single node, at 31 % mean CPU usage and 24.3 % memory usage.

Eight hours of observation processed in 8.7 hours is close to a 1:1 ratio between telescope time and processing time. That ratio matters for the SKA: as the volumes grow, processing has to keep pace with observation, and storage itself becomes a budget.

body.text: To make the DDF Pipeline ready for production processing of SKA data, effort has gone into documentation, multi-node robustness fixes, unit tests, and integration testing on the French supercomputers.
